issues.explanation: Pain Recall implies the patient personally sustained bodily injury during the trauma, which is hard to reconcile with the trauma type being trauma to a loved one unless there was also direct physical injury to the patient. That is not otherwise supported by the profile.

Physical Vulnerability and permanent bodily damage imply the patient believes his own body was physically harmed. For a trauma-to-a-loved-one presentation, this is difficult to explain clinically without evidence that he was also directly injured.

Military Topics is a trigger that suggests a military/combat-linked trauma context, but no other trigger, memory, threat, or appraisal item supports a military-related formulation. As a standalone item it feels disconnected from the rest of the profile.

Avoid Driving is plausible for motor-vehicle trauma, but here it lacks support from the trauma type and from the rest of the profile. With no transport-related trigger or memory content, it appears to target a symptom domain not otherwise represented.

For trauma to a loved one, visible injuries is a plausible trigger, but darkness and alcohol smell are not well anchored to the rest of the profile. Nothing in memory, threat, or appraisals suggests a dark-space or alcohol-related trauma context, so these triggers feel disconnected rather than part of a coherent loved-one trauma presentation.

Avoiding work/study is hard to reconcile with this patient's occupation as a paramedic unless the trauma is clearly tied to the workplace, but the rest of the profile frames the trauma as harm to a loved one rather than occupational trauma. Drug use is also insufficiently supported elsewhere in the profile: there are no other items indicating broad externalising coping or substance-related trigger context, making this strategy feel tacked on.

The rest of the profile does not provide supporting content suggesting he believes his own actions caused the loved one's trauma. The other appraisals are about damage and unreliability of self, so this item is the least integrated with the stated trauma type and surrounding node content.

Alcohol smell is not impossible, but in this profile it is the only trigger that suggests a substance-related context. The other trigger and memory items center on victims/injuries, which fits a paramedic exposed to injured loved ones or victims. Without any corresponding memory, threat, or appraisal content linked to alcohol, this item stands out as weakly connected to the rest of the trauma representation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Drug Use: take drugs
issues.explanation: Drug use can occur in PTSD, but here it is the only maladaptive strategy that implies substance misuse. The rest of the profile emphasizes work avoidance, suppression, sensory reliving, and hypervigilant threat responses. With no parallel alcohol/substance-related trigger, appraisal, or memory content, this item looks clinically disconnected from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, self-blame is plausible only if the patient had a clear perceived role in failing to protect or respond. In this profile, the other items describe reliving of victims/injuries, hypervigilance, and damaged-self beliefs, but nothing else indicates a responsibility-based trauma narrative. This makes the specific self-blame item the least coherent appraisal relative to the rest of the selected content.

vignette:
Amir was forty years old, a paramedic for over fifteen years, married with two children, and he had always thought of himself as someone who kept his head when others lost theirs. That ended on a Tuesday evening in late October, during a call that began as a routine response to a reported stabbing in a convenience store parking lot. His partner, Elena, was two years younger than him, quick-witted and steady, and they had worked together long enough to read each other’s movements without words. When they arrived, the scene was chaotic—a young man bleeding from a femoral wound, a woman screaming, bystanders filming on their phones. Amir knelt to apply pressure while Elena radioed for backup and began directing traffic. He did not see the second assailant emerge from behind the dumpster. He only heard the sound—a wet, hard crack—and then Elena was on the ground, her skull fractured by a steel pipe. He stayed with her, tried to stop the bleeding from her ear, but she was gone before the helicopter landed. In the weeks that followed, Amir could not stop the images from forcing their way in, but he learned to shove them back down. He told himself that dwelling on it would only make things worse, that the best thing he could do was keep moving and not let his mind wander to that parking lot. So he threw himself into his work with a ferocity that surprised even his crew. He volunteered for extra shifts, asked to be first on the rotation for the most difficult calls, and stayed late to restock the ambulance and clean equipment long after his shift ended. He wanted to be so exhausted by the time he got home that he would fall asleep before the memories could catch him, and for a few weeks it almost worked. But the effort of pushing the thoughts away was itself exhausting, and the images had a way of slipping through at the edges—the sound of a car backfiring in the station lot, the sight of a red stain on a uniform, the antiseptic smell of the emergency bay. He would feel his throat tighten and his heart race, and he would force himself to think about something else, anything else—the schedule, the weather, a joke he had heard—until the moment passed.

The cracks widened despite his best efforts. He began to notice gaps in his memory of the event itself: whole seconds he could not account for, like the time between hearing the crack and finding himself kneeling beside her. He tried to fill them in, but the effort only made the memories that did come back feel more vivid, more real, until remembering Elena’s face brought the same cold terror he had felt in that parking lot. He could no longer keep the thoughts at bay while on the job. Every visible injury, every wound he dressed or tourniquet he applied, was Elena’s wound. Every victim he tried to calm was her. The antiseptic smell of the hospital emergency bay—sharp and chemical—hit him like a physical blow, flooding his sinuses with the memory of the helicopter’s interior and the futile resuscitation. He began to dread his shifts, and within two weeks of the incident he started calling in sick. He would wake up on a Monday morning and feel his stomach clench, his heart race, and he would pick up his phone and leave a voicemail for dispatch—short, apologetic, a lie about a fever. The first time felt like failure; the tenth time felt like relief. He stopped answering calls from his supervisor. He stopped looking at the schedule when it was posted. He told himself he just needed a few days to clear his head, but the days turned into weeks. The station became a place he could not bear to imagine, let alone enter. He had come to believe that if he let himself go back, he would either break down in front of his crew or freeze on a call and let someone else die.

But the retreat from work bled into everything. He stopped attending the monthly training sessions at the firehouse because the classroom smelled like the hospital. He started sitting with his back to the wall in every room—at home, in his own living room, even when he went to the grocery store. If his wife touched his shoulder unexpectedly, he would flinch so hard he sometimes knocked her hand away. Concentration became a daily struggle: he would lose track of conversations mid-sentence, forget to eat lunch, drive past his exit on the way home. His wife noticed he was distant, irritable, and often wakeful; she assumed it was grief, and it was, but it was also something more tangled. Amir felt he had permanently changed for the worse, that the man who used to joke with his crew and sleep through the night was gone. Worse, he had begun to believe that he could not rely on himself any longer. If he had been more alert, if he had scanned the parking lot better, he could have seen the second man. He should have protected Elena. She was his partner, his responsibility, and he had failed. The thought sat in his chest like a stone, and no amount of staying home or keeping busy could dislodge it.

What finally brought him to seek help was a shift three weeks ago—the only one he had forced himself to take in over a month, partly out of guilt and partly because his supervisor had gently suggested he might be ready to try. He was assigned to a call for an elderly man who had fallen and gashed his forehead. The wound was minor, but when Amir leaned in to clean it, the sight of the torn skin, the hospital antiseptic smell from the man’s own bathroom, and the memory of Elena’s head all fused into one seamless, horrifying moment. He could not move. He stood frozen, his heart hammering, the room dissolving around him until a colleague touched his arm and he yelped, stumbling backward. After that, his supervisor called him in and told him to take medical leave. At home, alone with the silence, Amir finally admitted he could not keep going this way. He is afraid of what therapy might uncover—afraid that fully remembering will destroy him, or that he will discover he was never the man he thought he was. But he is also hoping, quietly, that there might be a way to live without the terror, without the constant watchfulness, without the crushing weight of having failed Elena, and without the shame of being a paramedic who can no longer go to work.
